geo.title: Get started
geo.body:
Swinging door: fix side AB and the angle at A, then swing a fixed-length 'door' BC from B. It hits the ray in two places.

  • I can build two different triangles from the same SSA data with compass and ruler.
  • I can explain why SSA is not a congruence test even when the sides are long.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: SSA can give two, one or no triangles, so it is not a test.

geo.title: The big idea
geo.body: SSA can give two, one or no triangles, so it is not a test.

geo.title: Worked example
geo.prompt: Swinging door: one SSA recipe, two triangles.

steps.step: Draw a ray from A. Mark B above it so that AB = 5 and the angle at A is fixed.
steps.reason: These are the given side and angle.

steps.step: Open the compass to the given length BC. Put the point on B and swing an arc.
steps.reason: Every point on the arc is that distance from B.

steps.step: The arc hits the ray twice. Call the points C1 and C2.
steps.reason: A circle can cross a line in two places.

steps.step: Triangles ABC1 and ABC2 have the same angle A, the same AB, and the same BC.
steps.reason: Same ray, same side, same compass setting.

steps.step: But AC1 = 3 and AC2 = 5, so the triangles are not congruent.
So SSA is not a congruence test.

figure.alt: One ray from A, one circle at B and two possible triangles: AB = 5, AC1 = 3, AC2 = 5.

slides.title: Try it
slides.html: Use the controls. A drawing suggests a result; it is not a proof.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Jordan says that if you make the lengths bigger, SSA becomes a congruence test.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

Keep the same angle at A, but make AB = 10. Draw the circle centered at B through the point 6 from A along the ray. That circle also crosses the ray 10 from A. So two different triangles have the same angle at A, the same AB and the same BC. Bigger lengths do not make SSA a test.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
In Worked example 1, which angle is included between AB and BC?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Angle ABC, not angle BAC.

Reveal second check

The two sides share the point B.

geo.title: Practice 1
geo.prompt: In Worked example 1, which angle is included between AB and BC?
geo.check: The two sides share the point B.

figure.alt: One ray from A, one circle at B and two possible triangles: AB = 5, AC1 = 3, AC2 = 5.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Do the two triangles in Worked example 1 have the same angle A?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Yes. Both use ray AB and the same ray from A.

Reveal second check

The two rays are exactly the same in both triangles.

geo.title: Practice 2
geo.prompt: Do the two triangles in Worked example 1 have the same angle A?
geo.solution: Yes. Both use ray AB and the same ray from A.
geo.check: The two rays are exactly the same in both triangles.

figure.alt: One ray from A, one circle at B and two possible triangles: AB = 5, AC1 = 3, AC2 = 5.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
Why does AC1 = 3 and AC2 = 5 prove the triangles are not congruent?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The other two sides match, but the third sides differ.

Reveal second check

Call the shared compass length r. The perimeters are 3 + r + 5 = 8 + r and 5 + r + 5 = 10 + r. They differ, so even changing the vertex matching cannot make the triangles congruent.

geo.title: Practice 3
geo.prompt: Why does AC1 = 3 and AC2 = 5 prove the triangles are not congruent?
geo.solution: The other two sides match, but the third sides differ.
geo.check: Call the shared compass length r. The perimeters are 3 + r + 5 = 8 + r and 5 + r + 5 = 10 + r. They differ, so even changing the vertex matching cannot make the triangles congruent.

figure.alt: One ray from A, one circle at B and two possible triangles: AB = 5, AC1 = 3, AC2 = 5.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html:
What condition gives one right triangle in the swinging-door picture?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The circle is tangent at the perpendicular foot from B, and that foot lies strictly past A on the ray. A single ray crossing is not always a tangency.

Reveal second check

Name the givens and the theorem or definition used.
